reviews.title: LÊ THỊ THANH HOA · IELTS 49 · W07 · Đề 1
reviews.overall: Em viết đúng đề, đủ bốn đoạn và nêu được Argentina tăng, Australia giảm, Thailand luôn đứng đầu. Cách chia theo nước có thể dùng được; số liệu trong hai đoạn Detail cũng cho thấy Argentina vượt Australia vào năm 2006. Tuy nhiên, phần Overview chưa nói rõ sản lượng Thailand tăng đến đỉnh năm 2006 rồi giảm. Ở Detail, em ghi sai số ô tô của Thailand năm 2003 và dùng “manufactured” để gọi nước sản xuất nhiều thứ hai. Bài còn lỗi số nhiều, mạo từ, chính tả và dấu cách quanh dấu câu. Cô yêu cầu em sửa và soát lại từng số với bảng.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em mô tả Thailand và Argentina trước, rồi dành đoạn Detail cuối cho Australia; cách chia theo đối tượng này phù hợp vì hai đoạn đều có ít nhất hai câu. Em đã nêu số đầu, giữa và cuối kỳ cho từng nước, nhưng nên làm rõ ngay trong Overview mốc đổi chiều của Thailand và sự đổi thứ hạng giữa Argentina với Australia.

reviews.originalEssay:
The table compares the number of cars produced in Argentina , Australia ,and Thailand in three different year : 2003 , 2006 and 2009. 
Overall , car production in Argentina saw a significant increase , whereas Australia experienced a steady decline over period . Additionally , Thailand consistently produced the highest number of cars among the three countries
In 2003 , Thailand led the figure with 735,825 car produced . This number rose sharply to peak at 1,162, 356 in 2006 , before dropping sightly to 999,963 in 2009 . In contrast , Argentina started with the lowest figure of 235,088 cars in 2003 . However , its production grew steadily to 352,759 in 2006 and reached 466,089 in 2009 , nearly doubling its intial amount . 
Regarding Australia , it was the second largest manufactured in 2003 , with 452,163 cars . However , the country experienced a continous decline , dropping to 341,268 in 2006 and further down to 245, 624 in 2009 , making it thee lowest producer by the end of period .

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The table compares how many cars were manufactured in Argentina, Australia and Thailand in 2003, 2006 and 2009.

Overall, car production rose steadily in Argentina and declined throughout the period in Australia. Thailand remained the largest producer in every year, although its output peaked in 2006 before falling. By that year, Argentina had overtaken Australia.

In 2003, Thailand produced 735,852 cars, far more than Australia, which made 452,163. Argentina had the lowest figure, at 235,088 vehicles. By 2006, Thai output had surged to a peak of 1,162,356 cars, while Argentina's figure rose to 352,759. Australia's production, by contrast, fell to 341,268, placing it below Argentina.

Over the final three years, Thailand's figure dropped to 999,963, but it was still higher than in 2003 and remained well above the figures for the other countries. Car production in Argentina continued to grow, reaching 466,089 cars in 2009, almost twice its initial total. Australia's output fell further to 245,624 cars, so Australia finished the period as the smallest producer despite ranking second at the start.

The line graph compares the proportion of female parliamentarians in five European nations—Germany, Italy, France, the UK, and Belgium—between 2000 and 2012.   
Overall, most countries experienced an upward trend in the percentage of women in parliament, with Italy eventually achieving the highest figure by the end of the period. In contrast, Germany remained relatively stable, while the UK started with the lowest proportion but recorded the most dramatic increase.   
To elaborate, Germany’s figure stood at roughly 33% in 2000 and showed almost no change throughout the 12-year timeframe. Italy began at 26%, steadily rose to 30% in 2004, and despite a minor drop, surged to peak at approximately 37% in 2012. Meanwhile, France started at 25%, peaked sharply at 36% in 2004, but later declined to around 29% by 2012.   
Regarding the remaining countries, the UK initially recorded the lowest rate at a mere 3% in 2000. After reaching 8% in 2004, it climbed steeply to hit 25% at the end of the period. Lastly, Belgium witnessed a substantial increase from 17% to 27% between 2000 and 2004, before dropping slightly to finish at 25% in 2012.

reviews.originalEssay:
The pie charts compare the main reasons why students selected a specific university in the UK in two different years, 1997 and 2007.  
Overall, having suitable degree courses remained the most significant factor influencing students' decisions over the ten-year period. Additionally, while course suitability, proximity to family, and teaching quality became more popular reasons, the importance of university resources and extracurricular activities declined.   
To elaborate, the proportion of students choosing a university due to suitable degree courses was highest in 1997 at 35%, and this figure increased slightly to 37% in 2007. Similarly, proximity to parental home saw a dramatic rise, more than doubling from 10% to 22% over the same period. The percentage of students prioritizing the quality of teaching also grew moderately, moving up from 15% in 1997 to 18% in 2007.   
Regarding the factors that experienced a downward trend, quality of resources accounted for 21% of student choices in 1997, but fell to 17% a decade later. Finally, the proportion of students motivated by good sports and social activities witnessed the steepest drop, plunging from 19% in 1997 to just 6% in 2007.

The table gives information and projections about the proportion of the population aged 65 and above in Canada, Germany, and the UK from 1988 to 2030.  
Overall, the percentage of senior citizens in all three countries increased over the first twelve years and is predicted to continue rising until 2030. Additionally, Germany consistently records the highest proportion of elderly people throughout the period, whereas the UK consistently shows the lowest figures.  
To elaborate, Germany had the largest share of citizens aged 65 and over in 1988, at 20.35%. This figure climbed to 25.53% in 2000 and is expected to reach a peak of 30.65% by 2030. Similarly, Canada experienced a steady upward trend, starting at 16.45% in 1988, growing to 20.65% in 2000, and it is projected to jump significantly to 26.35% by the end of the period.  
Regarding the UK, it accounted for the lowest percentage of older adults throughout the entire timeframe. In 1988, only 14.25% of the UK population fell into this age category, and this rate saw a slight rise to 14.80% in 2000. However, the proportion is forecast to experience a more substantial increase, reaching 20.45% by 2030.
